grey-basketball-jersey.fabricIntro: Standard sublimation polyester. For a grey game jersey we specifically recommend the moisture-wicking option rather than the base knit: grey shows sweat marks more than any other color, and a wicking fabric moves moisture to the outer face where it disperses.
grey-basketball-jersey.sizingIntro: Measure the chest at the fullest point with arms relaxed. Mid-grey sits between white and black visually, so it reads close to true to size where a light or dark jersey can look fuller or slimmer.
grey-basketball-jersey.bestForIntro: Grey is for third kits, showcases, alumni games and travel wear. As a primary home or away color it is unusual; most programs run it alongside a traditional pair.
grey-basketball-jersey.notFitIntro: For a league-mandated home or away kit, a traditional light or dark ground is the safer choice.

camo-basketball-jerseys.sub: A Pattern, Not a Color — Built So Numbers Still Read
prose: Camo is the one option here that is a pattern rather than a color, and that changes what has to be engineered. Camouflage is designed to break up shapes; a jersey number is a shape that must not break up. Printed carelessly, a camo jersey is genuinely hard to read from the bleachers.

The fix is structural. The number panel is printed as a solid block behind the numeral, or the numeral is given a heavy contrast outline, so the pattern runs across the jersey while the number stays legible. We proof camo designs at viewing distance rather than at desk distance for exactly this reason.

Most camo orders are for a reason rather than a season — military appreciation nights, veterans' games, and fundraising runs. Because sublimation has no per-color cost, a full multi-tone camo costs the same to print as a solid jersey, which is why one-off runs are practical here.

benefits.rest: — a solid panel or heavy outline behind each numeral, so the pattern never swallows it.
— camo that reads at a desk can be unreadable from the bleachers, so we check it the right way.

benefits.strong: Multi-tone costs the same as solid
benefits.rest: — sublimation has no per-color charge, so a full camo print is no more expensive.
— no setup charge per color makes a single appreciation-night kit affordable.

camo-basketball-jerseys.customizationIntro: Camo can be built in your team's colors rather than standard military tones — a navy-and-gold camo, or a red-and-black one — which is what most school programs actually want. Number panels, names and sponsor marks are placed so the pattern never compromises legibility.
camo-basketball-jerseys.fabricIntro: Standard sublimation polyester. A multi-tone pattern is no harder on the fabric than a solid color, because the entire design is laid down in a single pass regardless of how many colors it contains.
camo-basketball-jerseys.sizingIntro: Measure the chest at the fullest point, arms relaxed. A busy pattern reads slightly fuller than a solid ground at the same size, though not enough to change the size you order.
camo-basketball-jerseys.bestForIntro: Camo is for appreciation nights, fundraisers and alternate kits. As a regular game uniform it is unusual, and some leagues restrict patterns that interfere with number visibility — worth checking your rules first.
camo-basketball-jerseys.notFitIntro: Some leagues restrict patterned uniforms on number-visibility grounds. If yours does, a solid jersey with a strong accent is the safe route.

green-basketball-jersey.sub: The Widest Color Family in School Athletics
prose: Green covers more ground than any other team color. Forest, hunter, kelly, emerald and lime are not shades of one color so much as five different identities, and a program whose banners are forest green will not accept a kelly jersey. More green orders go wrong on shade than on anything else.

So the match comes first. Send a Pantone value, a school style guide, or a garment you already own, and that exact green is stored against your account and reused on every reorder. Guessing from a description — or worse, from a photograph on a phone screen — is how a set ends up two shades apart.

As a ground, green is easier to design on than it looks. White, gold and silver all read strongly against every green in the family, and a dark forest hides court marks nearly as well as navy while reflecting more heat than black does.

benefits.rest: — forest, hunter and kelly are different identities, and the match is made before anything prints.
— reorders in later seasons come back the same green, which is where most green orders go wrong.

benefits.strong: Gold and white read strongly on it
benefits.rest: — number contrast is straightforward across the whole green family.
— close to navy for practicality, with less heat absorption than black.

green-basketball-jersey.customizationIntro: The first decision is which green — send a Pantone number, a style guide, or a jersey you already own. Everything else prints full-color over that matched ground: accent panels, numbers, names, logos and sponsor marks.
green-basketball-jersey.fabricIntro: Standard sublimation polyester with the green dyed through the panel. Deeper greens absorb more heat than light ones; if your program plays outdoors regularly, a kelly or lime ground will run cooler than a forest one.

The difficulty is that orange sits where screens and fabric disagree most. A bright orange that looks right on a monitor frequently prints duller or browner than expected, so we match to a physical reference rather than a screen value, and store that reference for every reorder.

As a ground it is unusually loud, which is the point. Orange has the highest visibility of anything in a gym, and it takes navy, black and white accents cleanly. The one combination to avoid is a mid-yellow accent, which sits too close on the wheel to hold contrast from the bleachers.

yellow-basketball-uniform.sub: Gold and Yellow Kits, With Numbers That Still Read
prose: Yellow and gold are the brightest grounds in team sport, and they come with one specific engineering problem: a white or light numeral on yellow is almost unreadable from the bleachers. Contrast, not color, is what decides whether an official can call a number from the baseline.

The answer is a dark numeral or a heavy dark outline, and we treat it as a requirement rather than a style choice. Navy, black, forest and maroon numerals all hold their edge on yellow; we proof these designs at viewing distance so the decision is made against how it actually looks in a gym.

Ordering jersey and shorts as a set matters more here than on most colors. Yellow shows dye variation clearly, so a top printed now and shorts printed in three months are noticeably likely to sit a shade apart — printing both in one run is what keeps a gold set looking like one set.

benefits.rest: — a light numeral on yellow cannot be read from the baseline, so contrast is treated as a requirement.
— the number is checked the way an official sees it, not the way a designer does.

benefits.strong: Jersey and shorts in one run
benefits.rest: — yellow shows dye variation clearly, so a split order is how gold sets end up mismatched.
— a bright ground absorbs far less than black, which matters on an outdoor Florida court.

purple-basketball-jersey.sub: The Hardest Color to Reproduce, Matched Properly
prose: Purple is the color most likely to arrive wrong from a supplier, and it is worth understanding why. Screens make purple from red and blue light; fabric makes it from dye, and the two do not overlap cleanly. A purple that looks right on a phone can print noticeably more blue, or more maroon, than the program expected.

The only reliable answer is a physical reference. Send a Pantone chip, a school style guide, or a jersey you already own, and that becomes the standard — matched once, stored, and reused on every reorder rather than re-judged each time from a screenshot.

As a ground purple is genuinely strong. Gold, white and silver all read powerfully against it, and it occupies a space almost no other program in a given league will be using, which is worth something in a gym full of navy and red.

pink-basketball-jerseys.sub: Awareness-Game Kits, Practical as a One-Off Run
prose: Most pink basketball orders are not regular uniforms — they are awareness games, cancer fundraisers, and the one night a season a program plays in a different kit. That changes what matters about the order: it is a short run, it is on a fixed date, and it usually has to be paid for by the fundraiser itself.

Sublimation suits that shape of order well. There is no per-color setup charge, so a full-color pink kit with a ribbon graphic and a dedication on the back costs no more to print than a plain jersey, and a run of fifteen is economic in a way a screen-printed run of fifteen is not.

The practical detail programs miss is timing. An awareness game has a date that cannot move, so these orders need to be placed with real margin — we work backward from the game date rather than forward from the order date, and will say plainly if a date is not achievable.

benefits.rest: — a full-color awareness design costs the same to print as a plain jersey.
— a short run is affordable here in a way a screen-printed short run is not.
— individual back-of-jersey dedications add no cost, since it is all one print pass.
— an awareness date cannot move, so the timeline is built from it, not from the order date.
